title: Fictional workshop analysis
question: What would a fictional workshop need to cover its costs?
context: Entirely invented teaching example, adapted from benchmark A4. These are illustrative inputs, not observations about a live bookshop, actual customer demand or a real event. Ten paying attendees are assumed in every price scenario. No probability or recommendation to hold an event is asserted.
nextQuestion: What evidence would establish paying demand at a proposed price?

problem.situation: A fictional shop is considering one workshop and needs to distinguish arithmetic from demand evidence.
problem.desiredChange: Understand how price affects the result and identify what must be checked before a decision.
problem.constraints: All inputs are invented. Demand, capacity, extra staff costs and cancellation terms are not established. Prices are alternatives for sensitivity analysis, not a probability distribution.

nodes.label: Could the workshop cover costs?
nodes.notes: Separate conditional event economics from evidence of paying demand. The model answers a quantitative question under its assumptions; it does not establish attendance or support an event commitment.

nodes.label: Understand the event economics
nodes.notes: Net event result = (ticket price − variable cost per attendee) × paying attendees − fixed event cost. The attached workshop model has three invented price scenarios with the same assumed attendance. Prices can affect attendance in reality, which this simple sensitivity model does not capture.

nodes.label: Contribution after variable cost
nodes.notes: At the invented base ticket price of £20 and variable cost of £5, contribution is £15 per attendee. The Numbers model retains the calculation and basis.

nodes.label: Would enough people pay?
nodes.notes: The model assumes ten paying attendees; there is no evidence for that number or willingness to pay. Do not infer demand from the base scenario's positive result.

nodes.label: Inspect actual paid bookings
nodes.notes: In a real case, inspect available bookings and customer evidence at the relevant price before proposing a new experiment. No bookings or live source have been supplied in this fictional example.

decision.rationale: The arithmetic is illustrative. A decision to hold the workshop remains open because paying demand and complete costs are unverified.
uncertainties: Whether anyone would pay the proposed price.
Whether ten attendees and the stated cost structure are feasible.
nextSteps: Use actual evidence before replacing the invented inputs.

models.title: Workshop price sensitivity · invented inputs
models.description: One fictional event. Only ticket price varies: £15, £20 or £25. Attendance stays at an assumed ten in all scenarios. This isolates price sensitivity; it is not a demand forecast, an estimate of price elasticity or evidence that the high scenario is attainable.

variables.label: Paying attendees
variables.basis: Invented illustrative assumption: ten paying attendees in every scenario. No demand evidence supplied.

variables.label: Fixed event cost
variables.basis: Invented illustrative fixed cost. Cancellation treatment and additional staff costs are not established.

variables.label: Variable cost per attendee
variables.basis: Invented illustrative variable cost, assumed constant over the relevant attendance range.

variables.label: Ticket price
variables.basis: Invented price alternatives for a sensitivity calculation. They have no assigned probabilities and attendance is not adjusted for price.

variables.label: Contribution per attendee
variables.basis: Ticket revenue less variable cost; fixed event costs are deducted separately.

variables.label: Net event result
variables.basis: Assumed attendance multiplied by contribution, less the stated fixed cost. No additional benefits or costs are invented.

variables.label: Minimum attendees to cover costs
variables.basis: Round fixed cost divided by positive contribution UP to the next whole attendee. Here contribution is positive in each scenario. This threshold is not evidence that the attendees will book.

workplan.title: Check the scenario arithmetic
workplan.analysis: Calculate contribution, net event result and whole-attendee cost-covering thresholds for all three invented price scenarios.
workplan.evidenceNeeded: The explicitly labelled teaching inputs and the formulas in the workshop model.
workplan.source: Invented example inputs in this file; no live or external source.
workplan.priorityReason: Avoid mistaking an arithmetic error for a commercially meaningful result.
workplan.finding: At ten attendees, net results are −£20, +£30 and +£80. Minimum attendance is 12, 8 and 6 respectively under the stated model.
workplan.limitations: Completing this arithmetic check does not establish demand, completeness of costs or support for holding an event. Tree statuses remain unchanged.

workplan.title: Establish evidence of paying demand
workplan.analysis: In a real case, inspect existing bookings or customer evidence at the intended ticket price and before the commitment deadline.
workplan.evidenceNeeded: Paid bookings or sufficiently relevant customer evidence; distinguish stated interest from purchase commitments.
workplan.source: Not supplied. This example has no real booking records.
workplan.priorityReason: Attendance can reverse the conclusion even when the price and cost arithmetic is correct.
workplan.limitations: No real audience, price response, booking data or capacity figure has been established. No new experiment is automatically required.

brief.situation: A fictional shop is considering one paid workshop. The teaching model assumes ten attendees, £120 fixed event cost and £5 variable cost per attendee.
brief.complication: Paying demand is unknown. A positive result under an invented attendance assumption is not evidence that a real workshop will work.
brief.answer: The stated model gives a £30 base-scenario surplus at a £20 ticket price and ten attendees. Eight attendees cover costs at that price. Keep the event decision open until demand and complete costs are established.

sections.claim: The model is sensitive to ticket price when attendance is held fixed.
sections.body: At the same invented ten attendees, prices of £15, £20 and £25 produce net results of −£20, +£30 and +£80. This is a conditional comparison, not a forecast. A higher price may change attendance; this simple model does not estimate that response.

sections.claim: The event decision remains unresolved because paying demand is unknown.
sections.body: The eight-attendee base threshold describes the arithmetic. It does not show that eight or ten people will buy. Existing booking evidence, capacity and the completeness of the cost assumptions would change the decision.
